claim: LAR-type receptor phosphotyrosine-phosphatases (LAR-RPTPs) are presynaptic adhesion molecules that interact trans-synaptically with multitudinous postsynaptic adhesion molecules, including SliTrks, SALMs, and TrkC.
source: LAR-type receptor phosphotyrosine-phosphatases (LAR-RPTPs) are presynaptic adhesion molecules that interact trans-synaptically with multitudinous postsynaptic adhesion molecules, including SliTrks, SALMs, and TrkC.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature establishing these interactions.

claim: LAR-RPTPs are thought to function as synaptogenic wiring molecules that promote neural circuit formation by mediating the establishment of synapses.
source: Via these interactions, LAR-RPTPs are thought to function as synaptogenic wiring molecules that promote neural circuit formation by mediating the establishment of synapses.
evidence: This represents a hypothesis based on prior literature about LAR-RPTP function.

claim: Deletion of LAR-RPTPs had no effect on synaptic connectivity in cultured neurons or in vivo.
source: Strikingly, deletion of LAR-RPTPs had no effect on synaptic connectivity in cultured neurons or in vivo, but impaired NMDA-receptor-mediated responses.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript showing no changes in synapse density or connectivity measures.

claim: Deletion of LAR-RPTPs impaired NMDA-receptor-mediated responses.
source: Strikingly, deletion of LAR-RPTPs had no effect on synaptic connectivity in cultured neurons or in vivo, but impaired NMDA-receptor-mediated responses.
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological recordings showing decreased NMDAR-EPSCs in both cultured neurons and in vivo.

claim: Deletion of LAR-RPTPs decreased NMDA-receptor-mediated responses by a trans-synaptic mechanism.
source: Deletion of LAR-RPTPs decreased NMDA-receptor-mediated responses by a trans-synaptic mechanism.
evidence: This is supported by experiments showing that postsynaptic deletion of LAR-RPTPs had no effect, while presynaptic deletion did.

claim: Deletion of all LAR-RPTPs in cultured neurons led to a reduction in synaptic NMDA-receptor EPSCs, without changing the subunit composition or the protein levels of NMDA-receptors.
source: In cultured neurons, deletion of all LAR-RPTPs led to a reduction in synaptic NMDA-receptor EPSCs, without changing the subunit composition or the protein levels of NMDA-receptors.
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological recordings, Ifenprodil sensitivity experiments, and immunoblotting data.

claim: Deletion of all LAR-RPTPs in the hippocampus at birth did not alter synaptic connectivity as measured via AMPA-receptor-mediated synaptic responses at Schaffer-collateral synapses monitored in juvenile mice.
source: In vivo, deletion of all LAR-RPTPs in the hippocampus at birth also did not alter synaptic connectivity as measured via AMPA-receptor-mediated synaptic responses at Schaffer-collateral synapses monitored in juvenile mice, but again decreased NMDA-receptor mediated synaptic transmission.
evidence: This is supported by in vivo electrophysiological recordings showing normal AMPAR-mediated input-output curves.

claim: Deletion of all LAR-RPTPs in the hippocampus at birth decreased NMDA-receptor mediated synaptic transmission.
source: In vivo, deletion of all LAR-RPTPs in the hippocampus at birth also did not alter synaptic connectivity as measured via AMPA-receptor-mediated synaptic responses at Schaffer-collateral synapses monitored in juvenile mice, but again decreased NMDA-receptor mediated synaptic transmission.
evidence: This is supported by in vivo electrophysiological recordings showing decreased NMDA/AMPA ratios.

claim: LAR-RPTPs are not essential for synapse formation.
source: Thus, LAR-RPTPs are not essential for synapse formation, but control synapse properties by regulating postsynaptic NMDA-receptors via a trans-synaptic mechanism that likely involves binding to one or multiple postsynaptic ligands.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the lack of changes in synapse density and connectivity measures upon LAR-RPTP deletion.

claim: LAR-RPTPs control synapse properties by regulating postsynaptic NMDA-receptors via a trans-synaptic mechanism that likely involves binding to one or multiple postsynaptic ligands.
source: Thus, LAR-RPTPs are not essential for synapse formation, but control synapse properties by regulating postsynaptic NMDA-receptors via a trans-synaptic mechanism that likely involves binding to one or multiple postsynaptic ligands.
evidence: This is based on the observation that presynaptic but not postsynaptic deletion affects NMDAR responses, and the known interactions of LAR-RPTPs with postsynaptic partners.

claim: LAR-RPTPs are composed of a large extracellular sequence containing three immunoglobulin-like (Ig) domains and multiple (4-8) fibronectin-3 (FN3) repeats, and of a similarly large intracellular sequence containing two phospho-tyrosine phosphatase (PTP) domains.
source: LAR-RPTPs are composed of a large extracellular sequence containing three immunoglobulin-like (Ig) domains and multiple (4-8) fibronectin-3 (FN3) repeats, and of a similarly large intracellular sequence containing two phospho-tyrosine phosphatase (PTP) domains (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is established structural information about LAR-RPTPs, illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: LAR-RPTPs mediate essential functions in and outside of the brain during development.
source: LAR-RPTPs mediate essential functions in and outside of the brain during development (Elchebly et al., 1999; Uetani et al., 2006; Wallace et al., 1999), but are also highly expressed in mature neurons where they are thought to be presynaptic (Um and Ko, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: LAR-RPTPs are highly expressed in mature neurons where they are thought to be presynaptic.
source: LAR-RPTPs mediate essential functions in and outside of the brain during development (Elchebly et al., 1999; Uetani et al., 2006; Wallace et al., 1999), but are also highly expressed in mature neurons where they are thought to be presynaptic (Um and Ko, 2013).
evidence: This is based on expression data and a citation to previous work.

claim: Cell-adhesion interactions of LAR-RPTPs with numerous postsynaptic partners, including NGL-3, TrkC, SALMs, SliTrks, and IL1RAPs, suggest a major role for LAR-RPTPs in synapse formation.
source: Cell-adhesion interactions of LAR-RPTPs with numerous postsynaptic partners, including NGL-3, TrkC, SALMs, SliTrks, and IL1RAPs, suggest a major role for LAR-RPTPs in synapse formation (Choi et al., 2016; Kwon et al., 2010; Li et al., 2015; Lin et al., 2018; Takahashi et al., 2011; Takahashi et al., 2012; Um et al., 2014; Woo et al., 2009; Yoshida et al., 2012; Yoshida et al., 2011) (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is based on multiple citations to previous biochemical and structural studies.

claim: LAR-RPTP binding to postsynaptic partners is regulated by alternative splicing.
source: Moreover, LAR-RPTP binding to postsynaptic partners is regulated by alternative spicing, indicating a dynamic complex (Choi et al., 2016; Li et al., 2015; Yamagata et al., 2015a; Yamagata et al., 2015b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies on alternative splicing.

claim: In C. elegans, the LAR-RPTP ortholog PTP3 is expressed in two isoforms that differ in their extracellular domains.
source: In C. elegans, the LAR-RPTP ortholog PTP3 is expressed in two isoforms that differ in their extracellular domains.
evidence: This is established knowledge about C. elegans PTP3 from previous studies.

claim: The longer PTP-3A isoform is similar to vertebrate LAR-RPTPs, is specifically localized at synapses, and controls synapse morphology.
source: The longer PTP-3A isoform is similar to vertebrate LAR-RPTPs, is specifically localized at synapses, and controls synapse morphology (Ackley et al., 2005).
evidence: This is based on a citation to a previous study in C. elegans.

claim: The shorter PTP-3B isoform lacks the Ig domains as well as the first four FN3 repeats, and functions in axon guidance.
source: The shorter PTP-3B isoform lacks the Ig domains as well as the first four FN3 repeats, and functions in axon guidance (Ackley et al., 2005).
evidence: This is based on a citation to a previous study in C. elegans.

claim: Drosophila expresses two type IIA LAR-RPTPs, DLAR and Ptp69D, that have similar structures and are essential for axon guidance and for target recognition at neuromuscular junctions (NMJs) and at retinal photoreceptors.
source: Drosophila expresses two type IIA LAR-RPTPs, DLAR and Ptp69D, that have similar structures and are essential for axon guidance and for target recognition at neuromuscular junctions (NMJs) (Desai et al., 1997; Krueger et al., 1996) and at retinal photoreceptors (Clandinin et al., 2001; Maurel-Zaffran et al., 2001).
evidence: This is based on citations to previous studies in Drosophila.

claim: Loss-of-function mutants of DLAR in Drosophila exhibit smaller NMJs, larger active zones, and presynaptic release deficits.
source: Loss-of-function mutants of DLAR in Drosophila exhibit smaller NMJs, larger active zones, and presynaptic release deficits (Kaufmann et al., 2002).
evidence: This is based on a citation to a previous study in Drosophila.

claim: RNAi-mediated knockdowns of LAR-RPTPs in cultured neurons produced a massive loss of synapses and an impairment in neurotransmitter release.
source: RNAi-mediated knockdowns of LAR-RPTPs in cultured neurons produced a massive loss of synapses and an impairment in neurotransmitter release (Dunah et al., 2005; Han et al., 2018; Ko et al., 2015) consistent with a key role for LAR-RPTPs in synapse formation, but constitutive LAR-RPTP KOs did not cause gross abnormalities in the overall brain structure or evidence of synapse loss (Elchebly et al., 1999; Horn et al., 2012).
evidence: This is based on citations to previous RNAi studies.

claim: Constitutive LAR-RPTP KOs did not cause gross abnormalities in the overall brain structure or evidence of synapse loss.
source: RNAi-mediated knockdowns of LAR-RPTPs in cultured neurons produced a massive loss of synapses and an impairment in neurotransmitter release (Dunah et al., 2005; Han et al., 2018; Ko et al., 2015) consistent with a key role for LAR-RPTPs in synapse formation, but constitutive LAR-RPTP KOs did not cause gross abnormalities in the overall brain structure or evidence of synapse loss (Elchebly et al., 1999; Horn et al., 2012).
evidence: This is based on citations to previous constitutive knockout studies.

claim: Constitutive PTPRD and PTPRS KO mice exhibited reductions in body weight, postnatal lethality, and behavioral abnormalities that include ataxia, abnormal limb flexion, and memory deficits.
source: Constitutive PTPRD and PTPRS KO mice also exhibited reductions in body weight, postnatal lethality, and behavioral abnormalities that include ataxia, abnormal limb flexion, and memory deficits (Kolkman et al., 2004; Meathrel et al., 2002; Uetani et al., 2000; Wallace et al., 1999).
evidence: This is based on citations to previous constitutive knockout studies.

claim: Constitutive PTPRD and PTPRS KO mice display only modest changes of synaptic transmission, such as a reduction in presynaptic release probability and in LTP.
source: However, these mice display only modest changes of synaptic transmission, such as a reduction in presynaptic release probability and in LTP (Horn et al., 2012; Uetani et al., 2000).
evidence: This is based on citations to previous electrophysiological studies.

claim: Neither the single deletions of PTPRS, PTPRF, or PTPRD nor the triple deletion of all LAR-RPTPs altered the density of excitatory synapses.
source: Strikingly, neither the single deletions of PTPRS, PTPRF, or PTPRD nor the triple deletion of all LAR-RPTPs altered the density of excitatory (Figure 2A–B) or inhibitory synapses (Figure 2E–F).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data quantifying synapse density shown in Figure 2.

claim: Neither the single deletions of PTPRS, PTPRF, or PTPRD nor the triple deletion of all LAR-RPTPs altered the density of inhibitory synapses.
source: Strikingly, neither the single deletions of PTPRS, PTPRF, or PTPRD nor the triple deletion of all LAR-RPTPs altered the density of excitatory (Figure 2A–B) or inhibitory synapses (Figure 2E–F).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data quantifying synapse density shown in Figure 2.

claim: The size and staining intensity of vGluT1 and vGAT puncta were unchanged by LAR-RPTP deletions.
source: Moreover, the size and staining intensity of vGluT1 and vGAT puncta were unchanged by LAR-RPTP deletions (Figure 2C–D,G–H).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Deletion of all LAR-RPTP isoforms in a neuron did not induce detectable changes in dendritic arborization, axon length, and soma size.
source: However, deletion of all LAR-RPTPs in a neuron did not induced detectable changes in three basic morphological features (dendrites, axons, and cell body size), suggesting that LAR-RPTPs are not required for the basic development of neurons (Figure 2I–J).
evidence: This is supported by morphological analysis data shown in Figure 2I-J.

claim: Cultured neurons lacking individual LAR-RPTPs exhibit a normal capacitance and input resistance.
source: Using patch-clamp recordings, we found that cultured neurons lacking individual LAR-RPTPs exhibit a normal capacitance and input resistance, consistent with a lack of effect on neuronal development (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological measurements shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Deletion of all LAR-RPTP isoforms induced a small reduction (~15%) in neuronal capacitance, but did not affect the input resistance.
source: Deletion of all LAR-RPTP isoforms induced a small reduction (~15%) in neuronal capacitance, but again did not affect the input resistance (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological measurements shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Deletion of all LAR-RPTPs uncovered a significant decrease (~40%) in mEPSC frequency.
source: Recordings of spontaneous mEPSCs or mIPSCs from control neurons and neurons lacking all LAR-RPTPs, obtained as described above, uncovered a significant decrease (~40%) in mEPSC but not in mIPSC frequency (Figure 3A–B,D–E).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 3.

claim: Deletion of all LAR-RPTPs did not significantly change mIPSC frequency.
source: Recordings of spontaneous mEPSCs or mIPSCs from control neurons and neurons lacking all LAR-RPTPs, obtained as described above, uncovered a significant decrease (~40%) in mEPSC but not in mIPSC frequency (Figure 3A–B,D–E).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 3.

claim: Neither the mEPSC nor the mIPSC amplitudes exhibited major changes upon deletion of all LAR-RPTPs.
source: Neither the mEPSC nor the mIPSC amplitudes exhibited major changes (Figure 3C,F).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 3.

claim: A small but non-significant decrease in the amplitude of evoked AMPAR-mediated EPSCs was observed upon deletion of all LAR-RPTPs.
source: We also observed a small but non-significant decrease in the amplitude of evoked AMPAR-mediated EPSCs (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Evoked NMDAR-mediated EPSCs exhibited a major decrease in amplitude (~40% decrease) upon deletion of all LAR-RPTPs.
source: Evoked NMDAR-mediated EPSCs, in contrast, exhibited a major decrease in amplitude (~40% decrease; Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The NMDA/AMPA ratio was greatly decreased (~60%) upon deletion of all LAR-RPTPs.
source: As a result of the decrease in NMDAR- but not AMPAR-EPSCs, the NMDA/AMPA ratio was also greatly decreased (~60%; Figure 4C–D).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 4C-D.

claim: The selective impairment in postsynaptic NMDAR-mediated synaptic responses was not caused by a cell-autonomous postsynaptic function of LAR-RPTPs.
source: This selective impairment in postsynaptic NMDAR-mediated synaptic responses was not caused by a cell-autonomous postsynaptic function of LAR-RPTPs because postsynaptic deletions of LAR-RPTPs in sparsely transfected neurons had no effect on the NMDA/AMPA ratio (Figure 4E–F).
evidence: This is supported by sparse transfection experiments shown in Figure 4E-F.

claim: The current density of AMPAR-mediated responses was unchanged by the LAR-RPTP deletion.
source: The current density of AMPAR-mediated responses was unchanged by the LAR-RPTP deletion (Figure 4G, Figure 4—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is supported by bath application experiments shown in Figure 4G.

claim: The current density of NMDAR-mediated responses was significantly enhanced by the LAR-RPTP deletion.
source: Strikingly, the current density of NMDAR-mediated responses was significantly enhanced, and not decreased (Figure 4H, Figure 4—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is supported by bath application experiments shown in Figure 4H.

claim: The decrease in evoked NMDAR-EPSCs is not due to a loss of surface NMDARs, but is caused by a loss of specifically synaptic NMDARs.
source: This result indicates that the decrease in evoked NMDAR-EPSCs is not due to a loss of surface NMDARs, but is caused by a loss of specifically synaptic NMDARs.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that total NMDAR responses to bath application are increased while synaptic NMDAR responses are decreased.

claim: No major changes in NMDAR subunits, active zone proteins, or components of the neurotransmitter release machinery were detected upon LAR-RPTP deletion.
source: We detected no major changes in any protein examined, including NMDAR subunits, active zone proteins, or components of the neurotransmitter release machinery (Figure 5).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative immunoblotting data shown in Figure 5.

claim: No difference in Ifenprodil sensitivity was detected between control and LAR-RPTP KO neurons.
source: However, we detected no difference in Ifenprodil sensitivity between control (ΔCRE) or LAR-RPTP KO (CRE) neurons (Figure 4I–K).
evidence: This is supported by pharmacological experiments shown in Figure 4I-K.

claim: LAR-RPTPs are expressed at high levels in the hippocampus in both CA3 and CA1 pyramidal cells not only during development, but also in adult mice.
source: LAR-RPTPs are expressed at high levels in the hippocampus in both CA3 and CA1 pyramidal cells not only during development, but also in adult mice (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A) (Saunders et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by expression data from a single-cell RNA-seq database shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Presynaptic LAR-RPTP deletion caused a small but significant decrease in the frequency of sEPSCs.
source: Measurements of spontaneous sEPSCs (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B–C) and of unitary synaptic AMPAR-mediated events using Sr2+ in the extracellular medium (Figure 6B) showed that the presynaptic LAR-RPTP deletion caused a small but significant decrease in the frequency of sEPSCs, but had little effect on the amplitude of sEPSCs or of unitary EPSCs that reflects the size of AMPAR-mediated synaptic responses.
evidence: This is supported by in vivo electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B-C.

claim: Presynaptic LAR-RPTP deletion had little effect on the amplitude of sEPSCs or of unitary EPSCs.
source: Measurements of spontaneous sEPSCs (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B–C) and of unitary synaptic AMPAR-mediated events using Sr2+ in the extracellular medium (Figure 6B) showed that the presynaptic LAR-RPTP deletion caused a small but significant decrease in the frequency of sEPSCs, but had little effect on the amplitude of sEPSCs or of unitary EPSCs that reflects the size of AMPAR-mediated synaptic responses.
evidence: This is supported by in vivo electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 6B and Figure 6—figure supplement 1B-C.

claim: Input/output measurements as a function of electrical Schaffer-collateral stimulation demonstrated that the LAR-RPTP deletion caused no change in AMPAR-mediated synaptic strength or synaptic connectivity.
source: Moreover, input/output measurements as a function of electrical Schaffer-collateral stimulation demonstrated that the LAR-RPTP deletion caused no change in AMPAR-mediated synaptic strength or synaptic connectivity (Figure 6C), consistent with the lack of an effect of the LAR-RPTP deletion on AMPARs or synapse numbers observed in cultured neurons.
evidence: This is supported by in vivo electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The presynaptic deletion of LAR-RPTPs in CA3 neurons led to a significant reduction in the NMDAR/AMPAR ratio in CA1 neurons.
source: However, the presynaptic deletion of LAR-RPTPs in CA3 neurons led to a significant reduction in the NMDAR/AMPAR ratio in CA1 neurons (Figure 6D), similar to what we observed in hippocampal culture neurons (Figure 4C–D).
evidence: This is supported by in vivo electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 6D.

claim: A modest increase in the coefficient of variation (CV) of NMDAR-EPSCs, but not of AMPAR-EPSCs, was detected upon presynaptic LAR-RPTP deletion.
source: Furthermore, we detected a modest increase in the coefficient of variation (CV) of NMDAR-EPSCs, but not of AMPAR-EPSCs (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is supported by in vivo electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Deletion of all LAR-RPTPs in postmitotic neurons in vivo prior to synapse formation did not impede synaptogenesis, but caused a decrease in NMDAR-mediated synaptic responses without affecting AMPAR-mediated synaptic responses.
source: Viewed together, these data indicate that deletion of all LAR-RPTPs in postmitotic neurons in vivo prior to synapse formation did not impede synaptogenesis, but caused a decrease in NMDAR-mediated synaptic responses without affecting AMPAR-mediated synaptic responses.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the in vivo electrophysiological data.

claim: The presynaptic deletion of LAR-RPTP caused a large reduction in the NMDAR/AMPAR ratio when measured using optogenetic stimulation.
source: The presynaptic deletion of LAR-RPTP caused a large reduction in the NMDAR/AMPAR ratio (Figure 7B), confirming the results obtained with electrical stimulation (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is supported by optogenetic stimulation experiments shown in Figure 7B.

claim: LAR-RPTPs do not perform an essential role in synapse formation as such in vertebrate neurons.
source: Surprisingly, our results demonstrate that LAR-RPTPs do not perform an essential role in synapse formation as such in vertebrate neurons.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the lack of changes in synapse density and connectivity.

claim: LAR-RPTPs were not required for establishing or maintaining synaptic connections in cultured neurons or in vivo in a well-defined hippocampal circuit.
source: LAR-RPTPs were not required for establishing or maintaining synaptic connections in cultured neurons (Figures 2 and 3) or in vivo in a well-defined hippocampal circuit (Figures 6 and 7).
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on data from multiple figures.

claim: Single deletion of individual LAR-RPTPs or global deletion of all LAR-RPTPs did not change the number of excitatory or inhibitory synapses.
source: Specifically, single deletion of individual LAR-RPTPs or global deletion of all LAR-RPTPs did not change the number of excitatory or inhibitory synapses, did not induce alterations in axonal outgrowth or dendritic branching, and did not affect the synaptic connectivity of hippocampal Schaffer collaterals as measured by AMPAR-mediated input/output curves.
evidence: This is a summary of the morphological and electrophysiological findings.

claim: Single deletion of individual LAR-RPTPs or global deletion of all LAR-RPTPs did not induce alterations in axonal outgrowth or dendritic branching.
source: Specifically, single deletion of individual LAR-RPTPs or global deletion of all LAR-RPTPs did not change the number of excitatory or inhibitory synapses, did not induce alterations in axonal outgrowth or dendritic branching, and did not affect the synaptic connectivity of hippocampal Schaffer collaterals as measured by AMPAR-mediated input/output curves.
evidence: This is a summary of the morphological findings.

claim: Single deletion of individual LAR-RPTPs or global deletion of all LAR-RPTPs did not affect the synaptic connectivity of hippocampal Schaffer collaterals as measured by AMPAR-mediated input/output curves.
source: Specifically, single deletion of individual LAR-RPTPs or global deletion of all LAR-RPTPs did not change the number of excitatory or inhibitory synapses, did not induce alterations in axonal outgrowth or dendritic branching, and did not affect the synaptic connectivity of hippocampal Schaffer collaterals as measured by AMPAR-mediated input/output curves.
evidence: This is a summary of the in vivo electrophysiological findings.

claim: LAR-RPTPs do perform an important function in shaping synapse properties in mature neurons by controlling postsynaptic NMDAR-mediated responses.
source: However, our results demonstrate that LAR-RPTPs do perform an important function in shaping synapse properties in mature neurons by controlling postsynaptic NMDAR-mediated responses.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the NMDAR phenotype observed.

claim: The LAR-RPTP deletion caused a decrease in NMDAR-EPSCs that was due to a relative loss of NMDARs from postsynaptic sites and not to a decrease in NMDAR protein levels.
source: In cultured neurons, we showed that the LAR-RPTP deletion caused a decrease in NMDAR-EPSCs that was due to a relative loss of NMDARs from postsynaptic sites and not to a decrease in NMDAR proteins levels.
evidence: This is based on the observation that total NMDAR responses are increased while synaptic responses are decreased, and protein levels are unchanged.

claim: A large decrease in synaptic NMDAR-EPSCs evoked by action potentials was observed upon LAR-RPTP deletion.
source: We observed a large decrease in synaptic NMDAR-EPSCs evoked by action potentials, but a significant increase in NMDAR-responses elicited by direct NMDA application (Figure 4).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 4.

claim: A significant increase in NMDAR-responses elicited by direct NMDA application was observed upon LAR-RPTP deletion.
source: We observed a large decrease in synaptic NMDAR-EPSCs evoked by action potentials, but a significant increase in NMDAR-responses elicited by direct NMDA application (Figure 4).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 4.

claim: The decrease in synaptic NMDAR-EPSCs was likely due to a presynaptic mechanism since the postsynaptic LAR-RPTP deletion had no effect on NMDAR-EPSCs.
source: The decrease in synaptic NMDAR-EPSCs was likely due to a presynaptic mechanism since the postsynaptic LAR-RPTP deletion had no effect on NMDAR-EPSCs (Figure 4).
evidence: This is based on sparse transfection experiments showing no effect of postsynaptic deletion.

claim: The presynaptic LAR-RPTP deletion did not impair postsynaptic AMPAR-mediated synaptic responses in vivo.
source: The NMDAR phenotype was confirmed in vivo, where we demonstrated that the presynaptic LAR-RPTP deletion did not impair postsynaptic AMPAR-mediated synaptic responses, but decreased the ratio of NMDAR- to AMPAR-EPSCs (Figures 6 and 7).
evidence: This is supported by in vivo electrophysiological data shown in Figures 6 and 7.

claim: The presynaptic LAR-RPTP deletion decreased the ratio of NMDAR- to AMPAR-EPSCs in vivo.
source: The NMDAR phenotype was confirmed in vivo, where we demonstrated that the presynaptic LAR-RPTP deletion did not impair postsynaptic AMPAR-mediated synaptic responses, but decreased the ratio of NMDAR- to AMPAR-EPSCs (Figures 6 and 7).
evidence: This is supported by in vivo electrophysiological data shown in Figures 6 and 7.

claim: The LAR-RPTP function in regulating NMDARs resembles that of neurexin-1.
source: The LAR-PTPR function in regulating NMDARs resembles that of neurexin-1, suggesting a possible mechanistic convergence (Dai et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a comparison to previous findings on neurexin-1, supported by a citation.

claim: The well-described interactions of LAR-RPTPs with various postsynaptic adhesion molecules may, at least in part, control the properties of NMDARs.
source: These results indicate that the well-described interactions of LAR-RPTPs with various postsynaptic adhesion molecules (Choi et al., 2016; Kwon et al., 2010; Li et al., 2015; Lin et al., 2018; Takahashi et al., 2011; Takahashi et al., 2012; Um et al., 2014; Woo et al., 2009; Yoshida et al., 2012; Yoshida et al., 2011) may, at least in part, control the properties of NMDARs.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings in the context of known LAR-RPTP interactions.

claim: LAR-RPTPs' major function at the synapse appears to be to enable proper specification of synaptic properties, and not to mediate actual establishment of synapses and wiring of circuits.
source: Thus, LAR-RPTPs major function at the synapse appears to be to enable proper specification of synaptic properties, and not to mediate actual establishment of synapses and wiring of circuits.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the overall findings.

claim: It is possible that in addition to the robust effect of the LAR-RPTP deletions on NMDAR-EPSCs, the deletions also have an effect, albeit smaller, on release probability as suggested by their modest impact on mEPSC frequency.
source: It is possible that in addition to the robust effect of the LAR-RPTP deletions on NMDAR-EPSCs, the deletions also have an effect, albeit smaller, on release probability as suggested by their modest impact on mEPSC frequency, which would agree well with previous studies (Horn et al., 2012; Uetani et al., 2000).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the mEPSC frequency data.

claim: In hippocampal synapses, LAR-RPTPs are important determinants of synapse properties that contribute to regulating NMDAR mediated responses at synapses and thereby shape the properties of neural circuits.
source: Despite these limitations, however, our results indicate that in hippocampal synapses, LAR-RPTPs are important determinants of synapse properties that contribute to regulating NMDAR mediated responses at synapses and thereby shape the properties of neural circuits.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion of the study.
